The gas volume stayed the same.
The gas volume leveled off, then rose.

prompt: Lee takes a sealed can of juice from the refrigerator and sets it on the kitchen table on a warm, sticky summer day. Within a few minutes, the outside of the can is covered with tiny wet drops. Which process formed the drops?
explanation: Air holds water vapor as particles too small to see. When those particles touch the cold can, they slow down and gather into liquid drops. That is condensing.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the water came from ice on the can melting. A can from the refrigerator has no ice or frost on it; the drops come from water vapor in the air.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the cold can must have had ice on it that melted into drops

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: cold turns air itself into water by freezing it. Freezing would make ice, and the drops are liquid water that came from water vapor already in the air.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the cold can freezes the air and that makes the water

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the juice leaks out through the metal. The can is sealed and metal has no holes; the drops are plain water from the air, not juice.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the drink inside soaks out through the walls of the can

real_world_check: Water vapor in the air condenses into liquid water when it touches a cold surface, which is why a cold can gets wet on the outside.
key_category: a process that puts water on the outside of a cold container

prompt: Noor taps the water in a big tub with a pencil once each second, and ripples spread out across the tub. Then she taps three times each second, just as hard as before. What will most likely be different about the new ripples?
choices: The ripples will get across the tub sooner.
The ripples will be closer together than before.
The ripples will stand taller above the water.
The ripples will be spaced farther apart.
correct_answer: The ripples will be closer together than before.
explanation: The ripples still move at the same speed, but three start each second instead of one, so each ripple is only about a third as far behind the one before it. The ripples are closer together.

distractor_rationales.choice: The ripples will get across the tub sooner.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: making waves more often makes them travel faster. How fast ripples move depends on the water, not on how often Noor taps.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think tapping faster makes the waves themselves move faster

distractor_rationales.choice: The ripples will stand taller above the water.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: more taps make bigger waves. Height depends on how hard she taps, and she taps just as hard.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think more frequent waves must also be bigger waves

distractor_rationales.choice: The ripples will be spaced farther apart.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: more waves spread out more. With three ripples made each second moving at the same speed, each ripple has less room, so they are closer, not farther apart.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think making more waves pushes them farther apart

real_world_check: For waves moving at a fixed speed, making them more often (higher frequency) makes the distance between crests (wavelength) shorter.
key_category: a prediction about how water ripples change

This is the volume on day 6, one point too early.

passage: Rosa Valcourt wondered what helps salt vanish in water. She lined up two glass jars and two plastic jars on the counter. She gave one glass jar and one plastic jar twenty quick stirs and left the others alone. A timer showed how long each scoop took to disappear, and she asked whether stirring sped it up.
prompt: Which of these had only one value across Rosa's four jars?

refs.quote: Using her 200 mL measuring cup, she gave all four jars that volume of water

explanation: Every jar was filled with one 200 mL measuring cup of water, so the volume of water had a single value. Stirring, jar material and water temperature each had two values.

distractor_rationales.fault: Two jars got twenty stirs and two got none, so stirring had two values.
Two jars were glass and two were plastic, so the material had two values.
The glass jars held warm water and the plastic jars held cool water, so it had two values.

real_world_check: In an investigation, the conditions that are not being tested should have only one value so they cannot explain the results.

passage: Mateo dropped Ball Waddington from a height of 100 cm onto a hard floor. A friend filmed it beside a meter stick, and they played the video slowly to read the top of each bounce. The first bounce rose to 72 cm. The second rose to 52 cm, the third to 38 cm, and the fourth to 27 cm. They repeated the drop twice more, and each bounce came within 1 cm of these heights.
prompt: Which claim is NOT supported by Mateo's measurements?
choices: Each bounce reached a little under three fourths of the one before.
A fifth bounce would most likely reach less than 27 cm.
The fourth bounce rose less than one third as high as the drop.
Each bounce lost the same number of centimeters.
correct_answer: Each bounce lost the same number of centimeters.

refs.quote: The second rose to 52 cm, the third to 38 cm, and the fourth to 27 cm

explanation: The losses were 28 cm (100 to 72), 20 cm, 14 cm and 11 cm, so the ball did not lose the same number of centimeters on each bounce. The other three claims match the measured pattern.

distractor_rationales.choice: Each bounce reached a little under three fourths of the one before.
distractor_rationales.fault: This is supported: 72/100, 52/72, 38/52 and 27/38 are each about 0.72, a little under 0.75.

distractor_rationales.choice: A fifth bounce would most likely reach less than 27 cm.
distractor_rationales.fault: This is supported: every bounce was lower than the one before, so the pattern predicts a fifth bounce under 27 cm.

distractor_rationales.choice: The fourth bounce rose less than one third as high as the drop.
distractor_rationales.fault: This is supported: 27 cm is less than one third of 100 cm (about 33 cm).

real_world_check: A bouncing ball keeps roughly the same fraction of its height on each bounce, so the height lost per bounce shrinks and the pattern can predict later bounces.

prompt: A marble rolls across a smooth, level table at a steady speed and then rolls right off the edge. Which describes the marble's path after it leaves the table?
choices: It will move straight out, then drop straight down.
It will curve down as it moves forward.
It will drop straight down from the table's edge.
It will fall more slowly than a marble dropped from rest.
correct_answer: It will curve down as it moves forward.
explanation: Once the marble leaves the table, Earth's gravity pulls it downward while it keeps moving forward, so its path curves down to the floor.

distractor_rationales.choice: It will move straight out, then drop straight down.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: an object leaving an edge keeps going level until it stops and then falls, as in cartoons. Gravity pulls it down from the moment it leaves the table, so it curves at once.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a moving object keeps going level in the air before it starts to fall

distractor_rationales.choice: It will drop straight down from the table's edge.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: once nothing holds it up, an object loses its forward motion and falls straight down. The marble keeps its forward speed while gravity pulls it down, so it lands away from the table.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think things fall straight down as soon as nothing holds them up

distractor_rationales.choice: It will fall more slowly than a marble dropped from rest.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: moving forward holds an object up and slows its fall. Gravity pulls down the same either way, so it falls at the same rate as a dropped marble.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think moving sideways keeps an object up longer, slowing its fall

real_world_check: The gravitational force of Earth on objects is directed down, and an object moving sideways keeps its sideways motion while it falls.
key_category: a prediction of the path of a moving object

prompt: Kai holds a magnet over four objects on his desk: a new steel paper clip, an aluminum can tab, a copper wire and a small brass bell. Only the paper clip jumps up to the magnet. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The magnet pulls on steel, which has iron in it.
The clip was already a magnet all by itself.
The other objects are too big for this magnet.
Magnets pull every metal, but the clip is the thinnest.
correct_answer: The magnet pulls on steel, which has iron in it.
explanation: Magnets attract iron and materials that contain it, such as steel. Aluminum, copper and brass have no iron, so the magnet does not pull them.

distractor_rationales.choice: The clip was already a magnet all by itself.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: anything a magnet picks up must be a magnet too. A new steel clip is not a magnet; it is pulled because steel contains iron.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think that only magnets can be pulled by a magnet

distractor_rationales.choice: The other objects are too big for this magnet.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnets pull small things and fail only on large ones. Aluminum, copper and brass are not pulled at any size; size is not the cause.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a magnet fails to pull things only because they are too big

distractor_rationales.choice: Magnets pull every metal, but the clip is the thinnest.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnets attract all metals. Aluminum, copper and brass are metals that magnets do not attract.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a magnet will pull on any metal object

real_world_check: Magnets attract iron and steel (and a few other metals such as nickel and cobalt) but not aluminum, copper or brass.
key_category: an explanation of why a magnet pulls one object

passage: Priya set a ramp at one end of Track Murchison and put an empty paper cup on its side at the bottom. prompt: A fridge magnet holds one sheet of paper against a steel refrigerator door. Sam slips more sheets of paper under the magnet, one at a time, making a thicker and thicker pile. What will most likely happen?
choices: It will grip harder as sheets are added.
It will keep holding the pile no matter how thick.
It will fall the moment a second sheet goes under it.
After enough sheets, the magnet will slide off.
correct_answer: After enough sheets, the magnet will slide off.
explanation: Magnetic force passes through paper but gets weaker with distance. Each sheet pushes the magnet a little farther from the steel door, so at some thickness the pull can no longer hold the magnet and paper up.

distractor_rationales.choice: It will grip harder as sheets are added.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: more paper gives the magnet more to hold, so it grips harder. Each sheet moves the magnet farther from the steel, so its pull gets weaker.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a thicker pile gives the magnet a better grip

distractor_rationales.choice: It will keep holding the pile no matter how thick.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a magnet's pull does not depend on distance. The pull gets weaker as the gap between the magnet and the steel grows.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a magnet pulls equally hard at any distance

distractor_rationales.choice: It will fall the moment a second sheet goes under it.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: paper blocks magnetism. A magnetic force passes through paper; it only weakens gradually as the pile adds distance.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think paper or other materials stop a magnet from working

real_world_check: The force between a magnet and steel acts through paper without contact and becomes weaker as the distance between them increases.
key_category: a prediction of how a magnet behaves

passage: A small foil ball with an electric charge sat on a sensitive scale. Students charged Rod Quillan with the opposite charge and held it above the ball, so the rod pulled the ball upward and the scale reading dropped. They held the rod at five distances above the ball.

prompt: In a frost-free freezer, a fan blows very cold, dry air past an open tray of ice cubes. The freezer stays at -18 °C the whole time. After two months the cubes are much smaller, and there is no liquid water in the tray. Which process made the cubes shrink?
explanation: The ice went straight from solid to gas without melting, since the freezer stayed far below 0 °C and no liquid appeared. That change is sublimation.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: ice slowly thaws even in a freezer. At -18 °C ice cannot thaw into liquid, and no liquid formed; the ice turned straight into water vapor.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think ice can only shrink by thawing into water

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: ice dissolves into the air the way sugar dissolves in water. Ice does not dissolve in air; its particles leave the solid as a gas, a change of state.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think ice disappears into the air by dissolving in it

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: deposition is the solid-to-gas change. Deposition is the opposite, gas turning straight into solid frost; it would add ice, not remove it.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students mix up deposition with the solid-straight-to-gas change

real_world_check: Below its melting point, ice can turn directly into water vapor (sublimation), especially in dry moving air.
key_category: a change of state

prompt: The oxygen gas in the air is made of tiny particles that move about freely. Each particle is made of two oxygen atoms joined together. What is each of these particles?

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a particle is a tiny piece of the substance, like a small drop. A particle of oxygen is a molecule of two atoms, not a little drop of gas.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the particles of a gas are tiny drops or bits of that gas

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: particles of matter are little hard grains. A crystal is a repeating solid structure; oxygen gas is made of separate molecules moving freely.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students picture the particles of a gas as tiny solid grains

real_world_check: Oxygen gas is made of molecules, each of two oxygen atoms bonded together.
key_category: a particle that makes up a substance

prompt: When an apple drops from a tree, it falls toward Earth, but Earth does not seem to move up toward the apple. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Earth's huge mass barely changes its motion.
Earth pulls on the apple, but the apple does not pull on Earth.
Earth's pull on the apple is stronger than the apple's pull on Earth.
Gravity pulls on falling objects but not on objects resting on the ground.
correct_answer: Earth's huge mass barely changes its motion.
explanation: The apple and Earth attract each other with equal forces. The same force changes the motion of a small mass a lot and of Earth's enormous mass by an amount far too small to notice.

distractor_rationales.choice: Earth pulls on the apple, but the apple does not pull on Earth.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: gravity is one-way, from the big object to the small one. Every mass attracts every other mass; the apple pulls on Earth too.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think only the larger object does the pulling in gravity

distractor_rationales.choice: Earth's pull on the apple is stronger than the apple's pull on Earth.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the bigger object pulls harder. The two pulls are equal in size and opposite in direction.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a bigger object pulls a smaller one harder than the smaller pulls back

distractor_rationales.choice: Gravity pulls on falling objects but not on objects resting on the ground.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: gravity acts only on things that are falling. Gravity pulls on all matter, falling or not, including Earth itself.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think gravity only works on things that are up in the air or falling

real_world_check: Gravitational forces are attractive and act on both objects, and the same force changes a larger mass's motion less.
key_category: an explanation of motion caused by gravity

Mixing the liquids made a substance that was not there before.
The yellow solid was in one of the liquids all along.
Without any temperature change, a reaction cannot have taken place.
correct_answer: Mixing the liquids made a substance that was not there before.

prompt: Ocean waves roll past a pier. Their crests are 4 m apart, and 2 crests pass a post on the pier every second. A student multiplies 4 m by 2 per second and gets 8 m per second. What has she found?
explanation: Wave speed equals wavelength times frequency: 4 m times 2 per second is 8 m per second, which is how far a crest travels each second.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a wave's height and its speed are the same idea. Height (amplitude) is measured in meters from the rest level and is not found from spacing times rate.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think taller waves are faster waves, so height and speed go together

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: multiplying spacing by rate gives a time. Time between crests is the period, half a second here, not 8 m per second.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students mix up the period of a wave with its speed

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: frequency and speed are the same. Frequency is the 2 crests per second she started with; spacing times frequency gives speed.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think how often waves arrive is how fast they move

real_world_check: For any wave, speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency.
key_category: a quantity that describes a wave

prompt: An empty cup sits on a table with a coin on its bottom. Lea lowers her head until the coin just disappears behind the rim, then holds still. A friend slowly pours water into the cup without moving the coin. What will most likely happen?
choices: The coin will stay hidden behind the rim.
The coin will look bigger but stay out of sight.
She will begin to see the coin over the rim.
The water will block more of the light from the coin.
correct_answer: She will begin to see the coin over the rim.
explanation: Light from the coin bends (refracts) as it passes from water into air. The bent light can travel over the rim to Lea's eye, so the coin comes into view.

distractor_rationales.choice: The coin will stay hidden behind the rim.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: light always travels straight, even between materials. Light from the coin bends where it leaves the water, so it can reach her eye over the rim.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think light keeps going in a straight line through water and air

distractor_rationales.choice: The coin will look bigger but stay out of sight.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: water only magnifies things. The bending of light at the water surface changes the path, so the coin comes into view.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think water just makes things look bigger without changing where they appear

distractor_rationales.choice: The water will block more of the light from the coin.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: water blocks light, so things under water are harder to see. Clear water lets most light through and bends it toward her eye.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think clear water stops light the way a wall does

real_world_check: Light bends when it passes at an angle from water into air, so objects under water appear in a different place than they are.
key_category: a prediction about what a viewer sees

distractor_rationales.fault: This is about halfway between the 20 and 40 cm/s rows (13 and 27), the wrong pair of rows.
This is Penner's speed when Ludwick hit at 60 cm/s, faster than 50 cm/s.

prompt: Ana (40 kg) and her father (80 kg) stand still on ice skates, facing each other. Ana places her hands on her father's hands and pushes. What will most likely happen next?
choices: Both will glide apart, and Ana will move faster.
Her father will glide away, and Ana will stay put.
Both will glide apart at the same speed.
Both will glide apart, and her father will move faster.
correct_answer: Both will glide apart, and Ana will move faster.
explanation: Ana pushes on her father and he pushes back on her with an equal and opposite force. Both move apart; Ana has half the mass, so her speed is about twice his.

distractor_rationales.choice: Her father will glide away, and Ana will stay put.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: only the object that is pushed moves. Her father pushes back on Ana with an equal force, so she moves too.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the person who does the pushing does not move

distractor_rationales.choice: Both will glide apart at the same speed.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: equal forces give equal speeds. The forces are equal, but Ana has half the mass, so she gets the larger change in speed.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think equal and opposite forces must give equal speeds

distractor_rationales.choice: Both will glide apart, and her father will move faster.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the bigger person moves faster because he is stronger or heavier. The forces are equal, and the larger mass gets the smaller change in speed.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a bigger, heavier person gets a bigger result from a push

real_world_check: Forces come in equal and opposite pairs, and the same force changes a smaller mass's motion more.
key_category: a prediction of motion after a push

prompt: Ravi puts on a pair of dark sunglasses on a sunny afternoon. Everything he looks at now seems dimmer than before. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The lenses make his eyes send out less light.
The lenses absorb some of the light coming through.
The lenses bend the light so it misses his eyes.
The lenses add a dark color to the light passing through.
correct_answer: The lenses absorb some of the light coming through.
explanation: Tinted lenses absorb part of the light that hits them and let the rest through. Less light reaches Ravi's eyes, so everything looks dimmer.

distractor_rationales.choice: The lenses make his eyes send out less light.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: eyes send out light to see. Eyes only receive light; the lenses cut down the light that reaches them.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the eyes send out light, and seeing depends on it

distractor_rationales.choice: The lenses bend the light so it misses his eyes.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: sunglasses work by bending light away. Plain sunglass lenses hardly bend light; they absorb part of it.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think any lens works by bending light away from the eye

distractor_rationales.choice: The lenses add a dark color to the light passing through.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a tinted filter adds color or darkness to light. A filter can only remove part of the light; it cannot add anything to it.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a colored or dark filter adds its color to the light

real_world_check: When light hits a material, part can be absorbed and part transmitted; tinted lenses absorb a share of the light, so less reaches the eye.
key_category: an explanation of what sunglasses do to light

prompt: The students want to test only whether the mass of powder changes how cold a pack gets. Which pack should they compare with Pack Ostrander?
explanation: Pack Ostrander used 20 g of powder, 100 mL of water and a plastic pouch. Pack Thornbury used 40 g of powder with the same 100 mL of water and the same plastic pouch, so powder mass is the only difference between the two packs.

distractor_rationales.fault: It differs from Pack Ostrander in powder mass AND water volume (150 mL), so the effect of the powder alone cannot be separated.
It has the same 20 g of powder as Pack Ostrander; it differs only in pouch material, which is the wrong variable.
It differs from Pack Ostrander in powder mass and also in pouch material (foil), so two things change at once.

real_world_check: A fair comparison changes only one factor, so any difference in the result can be traced to that factor.

passage: A podcast club wants a foam cover for its microphone. Students slipped five foam covers, one at a time, over the same microphone. A speaker in front of the microphone played a recorded voice, and the recording app showed what percent of the voice got through compared with no cover. Then a desk fan blew across the microphone, and the app showed what percent of the wind noise got through. Table 1 shows the results.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Share of a voice and of wind noise passing through five microphone covers

prompt: The cover must let through at least 80% of the voice and less than 30% of the wind noise. Based on Table 1, which cover meets both requirements?
explanation: Cover Ballard passes 88% of the voice, which is at least 80%, and 22% of the wind noise, which is under 30%. Every other cover fails one of the two limits.

distractor_rationales.fault: It passes 85% of the voice, but 42% of the wind noise, above the 30% limit.
It blocks wind well (18%), but passes only 74% of the voice, below 80%.
It passes 92% of the voice, but 35% of the wind noise, above the 30% limit.

real_world_check: Sound striking a material is partly transmitted and partly absorbed or reflected; different materials pass different shares of different sounds.

prompt: A heater gives the same amount of energy to a 100 g cup of water and to a 400 g pot of water. Both start at 20 °C, and no energy escapes. Which quantity ends up greater for the water in the cup than for the water in the pot?
explanation: The same energy is shared by four times as much water in the pot, so the pot warms by about one quarter as much. The cup ends up at a higher temperature. Temperature measures the average motion energy of the particles, not the total thermal energy.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the hotter sample holds more thermal energy. The 400 g pot holds far more particles and ends up with more total thermal energy than the 100 g cup.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think whichever sample is hotter must hold more thermal energy

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: heating packs water particles closer together. Warmer water is slightly LESS dense, so the hotter cup does not have the greater density.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think heating water squeezes its particles together so it gets denser

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: particles swell when heated. Water molecules do not grow; heating makes them move faster and spread a little, so particle size is the same in both.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the particles themselves get bigger when a substance is heated

real_world_check: Adding the same energy to a smaller mass of the same substance produces a larger temperature rise (MS-PS3-4).
key_category: a quantity that describes a sample of water

prompt: A wooden crate sits loose on the flat bed of a pickup truck. The truck is driving forward when the driver brakes hard. The crate slides toward the front of the truck bed. Which statement best explains why the crate slides forward?
choices: Braking creates a forward force on the crate that pushes it toward the cab.
The crate carries a force of motion that drives it ahead.
The brakes push the truck back and the crate forward.
The crate keeps moving forward while the truck under it slows down.
correct_answer: The crate keeps moving forward while the truck under it slows down.
explanation: An object keeps moving at the same speed and direction unless an unbalanced force acts on it. When the truck slows, the loose crate is not slowed as quickly, so it keeps going forward relative to the truck bed.

distractor_rationales.choice: Braking creates a forward force on the crate that pushes it toward the cab.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: something moving forward must be pushed by a forward force. No forward force acts; the crate simply keeps its motion while friction is too weak to slow it as fast as the truck.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think an object that moves forward must have a forward force pushing it

distractor_rationales.choice: The crate carries a force of motion that drives it ahead.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a moving object stores a "force of motion" (impetus). Motion continues without any force; there is no stored force inside the crate.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a moving object carries a force inside it that keeps it going

distractor_rationales.choice: The brakes push the truck back and the crate forward.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: action and reaction act on the same pair of objects here. The brakes act on the wheels, not on the crate; nothing pushes the crate forward.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think braking pushes the vehicle one way and its cargo the other way

real_world_check: With no net force, an object keeps its velocity; friction from the bed is the only horizontal force on the crate and it acts backward.
key_category: an explanation of why a loose object moves relative to a braking vehicle

prompt: The Moon moves very fast along its path, yet it keeps circling Earth instead of flying off into space. Which statement best explains why the Moon stays in orbit?
choices: Earth's gravity keeps pulling on the Moon and bends its path into a curve.
Earth's magnetism holds the Moon the way a magnet holds a steel ball.
Space has no gravity to pull the Moon away from Earth.
The Moon's own spinning holds it on a circle around Earth and keeps it from drifting off.
correct_answer: Earth's gravity keeps pulling on the Moon and bends its path into a curve.
explanation: The Moon's speed would carry it off in a straight line, but Earth's gravity pulls it toward Earth all the time. That pull bends its straight path into a curve that wraps around Earth.

distractor_rationales.choice: Earth's magnetism holds the Moon the way a magnet holds a steel ball.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: gravity is a kind of magnetism. The Moon is not held by magnetism; gravity acts between any two masses, magnetic or not.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think Earth's magnetism is what holds the Moon in place

distractor_rationales.choice: Space has no gravity to pull the Moon away from Earth.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: there is no gravity in space. Gravity reaches through space; Earth's gravity is what keeps the Moon near Earth.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think there is no gravity in space so things just float there

distractor_rationales.choice: The Moon's own spinning holds it on a circle around Earth and keeps it from drifting off.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: spinning keeps an object in orbit. The Moon's spin on its axis does not curve its path; only a force toward Earth does.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think spinning is what keeps a moon or planet going around in a circle

real_world_check: Gravity is an attractive force between masses; a sideways velocity plus a constant pull toward the center produces an orbit.
key_category: an explanation of why a moon stays in orbit around a planet

passage: Students glued five kinds of sole rubber, one at a time, to the bottom of a 2 kg block. They pulled the block across a gym floor with a spring scale and read the force needed to start it sliding.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Pull needed to start a 2 kg block sliding on a gym floor

prompt: A dance studio wants a sole that needs more than 30 N to start sliding, so dancers do not slip, but less than 45 N, so they can still turn. Based on Figure 1, which sole meets both needs?
explanation: Sole Varga's bar is between the 30 N and 45 N ticks (about 38 N). Sole Iko and Sole Ellsworth are below 30 N, and Sole Holcomb and Sole Quimper are above 45 N.

distractor_rationales.fault: Its bar is below the 30 N tick (about 22 N), so it slips too easily.
Its bar is above the 45 N tick (about 52 N), so it grips too much to turn.
Its bar is the shortest, well under 30 N, so it slips too easily.

real_world_check: Friction between two surfaces depends on the materials in contact; a design criterion with two limits needs a value between them.

passage: Marisol warmed 250 mL of skim milk and stirred in 20 mL of vinegar. White lumps formed in the liquid. She poured the mix through a cloth, pressed the lumps into a mold and let them dry for two days. The dry material was hard and slightly bendable. Then she compared it with milk. Milk poured onto a tile spread out flat, but the new material stayed in its molded form. A drop of water soaked into a paper towel at once but beaded up on the new material. Milk boiled at about 100 °C on a hot plate. A chip of the new material did not melt or boil on the hot plate; it turned brown and smelled burnt.
prompt: Which claim is supported by Marisol's results?
choices: The material was made from a resource that is not natural.
The new material soaks up water faster than paper does.
Unlike milk, it holds its own shape.
It melts at a lower temperature than milk boils.
correct_answer: Unlike milk, it holds its own shape.

refs.quote: Milk poured onto a tile spread out flat, but the new material stayed in its molded form.

explanation: Milk spread out flat on the tile, while the dry material stayed in its molded form. That difference in a property is exactly what the claim states.

distractor_rationales.choice: The material was made from a resource that is not natural.
distractor_rationales.fault: Not supported: it was made from milk and vinegar, which come from natural sources.

distractor_rationales.choice: The new material soaks up water faster than paper does.
distractor_rationales.fault: Not supported: the drop beaded up on the material but soaked into the paper towel at once.

distractor_rationales.choice: It melts at a lower temperature than milk boils.
distractor_rationales.fault: Not supported: the chip never melted on the hot plate; it browned and burned instead.

real_world_check: Synthetic materials are made from natural resources and have properties different from the starting materials (MS-PS1-3).

passage: Students slid Ring Magnets RX-5 onto a wooden dowel with like poles facing, so the top magnet floated above the bottom one. They pushed the top magnet down to a set gap, let go and measured how high it jumped.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Jump height of the top magnet after release from five gaps

prompt: Based on Table 1, how much higher did the top magnet jump when let go from a 6 mm gap than from a 10 mm gap?
explanation: From a 6 mm gap the magnet jumped 13.6 cm; from a 10 mm gap it jumped 5.1 cm. 13.6 - 5.1 = 8.5 cm.

distractor_rationales.fault: Subtracts the 8 mm row (8.3 cm) from the 6 mm row instead of the 10 mm row.
Reads the 6 mm jump height alone without subtracting the 10 mm height.
Subtracts the 6 mm row from the 4 mm row (22.8 - 13.6), the wrong pair of gaps.

real_world_check: Pushing repelling magnets closer stores more potential energy in the magnetic field, which becomes motion when released.
prior_free: MS-PS3-2 says repelling magnets pushed closer store more energy, but not by how many centimeters the jump grows from 10 mm to 6 mm; only the table gives 5.1 and 13.6.

passage: Students placed Block Magnets QM-2 with opposite poles facing on a track and used a force sensor to measure the pull between them at several gaps.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Pull between two block magnets at five gaps

prompt: Based on Table 1, which value is closest to the pull the students would most likely measure at a gap of 3 cm?
explanation: A 3 cm gap lies between the 2 cm row (5.8 N) and the 4 cm row (2.2 N), so the pull must be between 2.2 N and 5.8 N. Halfway is about 4.0 N, the only choice in that range.

distractor_rationales.fault: Lies below the 4 cm value (2.2 N); a 3 cm gap is closer than 4 cm, so the pull must be greater than 2.2 N.
Reads the 4 cm row; the magnets are closer at 3 cm, so the pull is larger than this.
Reads the 6 cm row, far from a 3 cm gap.

real_world_check: The force between two magnets weakens as the distance between them grows (MS-PS2-3).
prior_free: MS-PS2-3 says magnets pull less when farther apart, but not how large this pull is at 3 cm; only the 2 cm and 4 cm rows bracket it.

passage: Students warmed 100 g batches of four kinds of metal pellets to 90 °C in a water bath. They poured each batch into its own foam cup holding 100 g of cool tap water, stirred, and read the water before pouring and again once it stopped warming.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Water readings before and after hot metal pellets were poured in

prompt: Based on Table 1, which batch of pellets warmed its cup of water by the largest amount?
explanation: The rises are Vey 8 °C, Tesca 25 - 12 = 13 °C, Gorrell 9 °C and Pettibone 6 °C. The Tesca batch warmed its water the most even though its cup did not end the warmest.

distractor_rationales.fault: Its water warmed from 15 °C to 23 °C, a rise of 8 °C, less than the 13 °C of the key batch.
Its water ended warmest (28 °C), but it started at 19 °C, so it rose only 9 °C.
Its water warmed from 17 °C to 23 °C, a rise of only 6 °C.

real_world_check: Thermal energy moves from hot metal to cooler water; equal masses of different metals at one temperature give the water different amounts of energy.

passage: Students let five hammer heads fall onto a nail from a set height. From how far the nail sank into a pine board, they worked out how much energy each hammer gave the nail.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Energy five falling hammer heads gave to a nail

prompt: Based on Figure 1, about how much energy did Hammer Harlan give the nail?
explanation: Hammer Harlan's bar is the tallest and reaches the top tick of the axis, 18 J.

distractor_rationales.fault: This is the shortest bar, Hammer Penrod, not Hammer Harlan.
Hammer Harlan reaches the top tick of the axis; 13 J would sit below the tick near 13.5.
This is the height of Hammer Biel, not Hammer Harlan.

real_world_check: A falling hammer transfers its motion energy to the nail it strikes (MS-PS3-5).

passage: Students stirred together the two liquids of Resin Kit DV-7, a craft plastic made from chemicals refined from oil, and poured the blend into a mold. Every 2 hours they pressed a hardness tester into the surface.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Hardness of a two-part craft resin as it set

prompt: Based on Figure 1, about what hardness reading did the resin have 8 hours after stirring?
explanation: The line rises and then levels off at the top tick; at 8 hours it reads 60 units.

distractor_rationales.fault: This is the reading right after stirring, at 0 hours, while the resin was still liquid.
This is the reading at 2 hours, not 8 hours.
The line passes 45 units between 2 and 4 hours; by 8 hours it sits at the top tick.

real_world_check: Synthetic materials such as resins are made from natural resources by chemical processes; the stirred liquids react to form a hard solid.
prior_free: MS-PS1-3 says synthetic materials come from chemical processes, but not how hard this resin gets or when it stops hardening; only the graph shows it.

passage: Students fixed Fan Unit HB-9 to a cart and tilted its blades to different angles. For each angle, they ran the cart down a long, level track and recorded its top speed.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Top speed of a fan cart at seven blade angles

prompt: Based on Figure 1, how did the top speed of the cart change as the blade angle increased from 10 degrees to 70 degrees?
choices: The top speed rose, then fell.
The top speed decreased, then rose.
correct_answer: The top speed rose, then fell.
explanation: The points climb from 32 cm/s at 10 degrees to 70 cm/s at 40 degrees, then drop to 22 cm/s at 70 degrees.

distractor_rationales.fault: The top speed climbed from 32 cm/s to 70 cm/s before it dropped, so it did not only fall.
After 40 degrees the top speed dropped to 22 cm/s, so it did not only increase.

distractor_rationales.fault: The order is reversed: the speed went up first, peaked near 40 degrees, then went down.

passage: Students made waves in Tank Ardagh, a long tank of water, by dipping a paddle at one end two times each second. Upright rulers stood in the water at five distances from the paddle. A phone filmed each wave as it passed the rulers. Later the students paused the video and read the height of the crest above the calm water level at each ruler. They ran the test with the paddle dipped 2 cm into the water and again with it dipped 5 cm. Table 1 shows the results.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Height of a wave crest at five distances for two paddle dips

prompt: Based on Table 1, how tall was the crest 60 cm from the paddle when the paddle was dipped 5 cm?
explanation: In the row "60 cm from paddle" and the column for the 5 cm dip, the table reads 20 mm.

distractor_rationales.fault: This is the 5 cm dip at 80 cm from the paddle, one row too far.
This is the 2 cm dip at 60 cm, the wrong column.
This is the 2 cm dip at 20 cm, the wrong row and the wrong column.

prompt: A ball-and-stick model shows one large black ball joined to two small white balls. Each color stands for a different element, and the three joined balls move together as one unit. What does the model show?
explanation: The atoms are bonded and move as one unit, so the model is a molecule. Because the atoms come from two different elements, it is a molecule of a compound.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: atoms that join become one bigger atom. Joined atoms keep their identity; three atoms bonded together make a molecule, not an atom.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think atoms that stick together melt into one larger atom

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: two kinds of atoms together must be a mixture. In a mixture the parts are not bonded; here the atoms are joined and move as one unit, so it is a compound.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think anything with two kinds of atoms in it is a mixture

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: any molecule is an element. A molecule of an element has only one kind of atom; this one has two kinds.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think every molecule counts as an element because it is a pure particle

real_world_check: A molecule is a group of bonded atoms; if the atoms are of two or more elements, the substance is a compound.
key_category: a kind of particle that makes up matter

prompt: At night, with the lamps on inside, Jae sees a clear image of his room in the living-room window. On a sunny afternoon he sees the yard through the same window and barely any image of the room. Which statement best explains the difference?
choices: At night the glass reflects a bigger share of the light that strikes it.
In the dark, glass stops letting light through.
By day, brighter sunshine from the yard swamps the faint image.
In daylight the glass soaks up the light coming from inside the room before it can bounce back.
correct_answer: By day, brighter sunshine from the yard swamps the faint image.
explanation: Glass always bounces back a small part of the room light toward Jae. By day, far brighter light from the yard passes through the glass toward him and swamps that faint image; at night little outdoor light comes through, so the image is easy to see.

distractor_rationales.choice: At night the glass reflects a bigger share of the light that strikes it.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: glass turns into a mirror in the dark. The glass reflects the same small share of light day or night; only the light coming through from outside changes.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think glass becomes more like a mirror when it is dark outside

distractor_rationales.choice: In the dark, glass stops letting light through.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: glass only passes light when it is light out. Glass passes light at night too; there is simply little outdoor light to pass.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a window only lets light through during the day

distractor_rationales.choice: In daylight the glass soaks up the light coming from inside the room before it can bounce back.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: sunlight makes the glass absorb the room light. Clear glass absorbs very little light at any time; the image is still there by day but is drowned out.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think sunshine makes window glass soak up light instead of bouncing it back

real_world_check: Clear glass reflects a few percent of incident light and transmits most of it, in daylight and at night alike.
key_category: an explanation of when a mirror image in a window can be seen

passage: Students cut slices from one apple and set them on five plates. On some plates they brushed the slices with lemon juice. explanation: Plate Esterly had no lemon juice, sat on the counter and held a 5 mm slice. Plate Wetherall had lemon juice, sat on the counter and held a 5 mm slice, so lemon juice is the only difference.

distractor_rationales.fault: It had no lemon juice, like Plate Esterly; it differs only in storage, the wrong variable.
It had lemon juice but was also stored in the fridge, so two things differ from Plate Esterly at once.
It had lemon juice but its slice was 10 mm thick, so two things differ from Plate Esterly at once.

real_world_check: A color change from a reaction with oxygen is evidence of a new substance; a fair comparison changes only one factor.

passage: Students poured 500 mL of 20 °C water into five pans of one size and shape whose bases were made of different metals. They heated each pan on the same electric burner and timed how long the water took to start boiling.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Time for 500 mL of water to boil in five pans on one burner

prompt: Based on Figure 1, which pan passed thermal energy from the burner into the water at the greatest rate?

The class tried settings 1, 2 and 3, so this took three values.
The turbine sat 25 cm, 50 cm and 100 cm from the fan, so this took three values.

Each pulse took about 1.6 seconds to cross the spring.
Pulses from the wider sweeps reached the cup in less time than the others.
Sweep width made little difference to travel time.
correct_answer: Pulses from the wider sweeps reached the cup in less time than the others.

prompt: A student lists pushes and pulls that work across a gap, with no contact. Which of these is caused by an electric force?
explanation: Combing hair moves electric charge onto the comb, and the charged comb pulls bits of paper toward it without touching them. That pull is an electric force.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnets pull because they carry electric charge. A magnet acts by a magnetic force; an uncharged magnet still lifts steel pins.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think magnets work by static electricity or electric charge

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a compass is turned by electric charge in the ground. A compass needle is turned by Earth's magnetic field, a magnetic force.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a compass needle is pushed by electricity in the Earth

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: Earth pulls falling objects with an electric pull. Falling objects are pulled by gravity, which acts between masses whether or not they are charged.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think Earth pulls things down with a kind of electric or magnetic pull

real_world_check: Electric forces act between charged objects at a distance; magnetic and gravitational forces also act at a distance but are different forces.
key_category: an example of a force that acts across a gap

prompt: After a rain shower, a puddle forms on a sidewalk. By late afternoon on a warm day the puddle is gone. No one swept it away, and the sidewalk is sealed so water cannot soak in. Which statement best explains what happened to the water?
choices: Its fastest particles broke free from the surface and mixed into the air as a gas.
The sun's heat split the water into hydrogen and oxygen gas.
The water particles shrank until they were too small to exist.
The water changed into air and became part of the wind.
correct_answer: Its fastest particles broke free from the surface and mixed into the air as a gas.
explanation: Particles at the surface of a liquid are always moving at a range of speeds. The fastest ones escape into the air as water vapor, and on a warm day enough of them escape for the whole puddle to evaporate.

distractor_rationales.choice: The sun's heat split the water into hydrogen and oxygen gas.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: evaporation breaks water apart into its elements. Water molecules leave the puddle whole as water vapor; splitting water needs a chemical reaction.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think evaporating water breaks down into hydrogen and oxygen

distractor_rationales.choice: The water particles shrank until they were too small to exist.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: matter can shrink away to nothing. The particles stay the same size and still exist, now spread through the air.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think water that evaporates just disappears and stops existing

distractor_rationales.choice: The water changed into air and became part of the wind.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: water turns into air. Water vapor is still water; it mixes with the gases of the air but does not become them.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think evaporated water turns into air itself

prompt: Lena rides her bike fast along a flat path, then squeezes the hand brakes hard and stops. What will most likely happen to the energy of the bike's motion as she stops?

It flows back into Lena's legs as the energy she used to pedal.
correct_answer: It warms the brake pads and the wheel rims.

distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a stopped object still holds the energy it had while moving

distractor_rationales.choice: It flows back into Lena's legs as the energy she used to pedal.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: energy returns to where it came from. The brakes rub on the rims; the energy goes into warming them, not back into her body.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think energy flows back to its source when the motion ends

real_world_check: When the kinetic energy of an object decreases, energy is transferred out of it, here as thermal energy through friction (MS-PS3-5).
key_category: a prediction of where a moving object's energy goes when it stops

prompt: On a cold winter day, Mina stays warm in a puffy jacket filled with down feathers. Which statement best explains how the jacket keeps her warm?

The puffy layer blocks the cold from flowing in to her skin.

The jacket soaks up warmth from the cold outside air and then passes that warmth on to her.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: clothing makes its own heat. Feathers produce no thermal energy; the warmth comes from her body.

distractor_rationales.choice: The puffy layer blocks the cold from flowing in to her skin.

distractor_rationales.misconception: students think cold flows into the body the way heat flows out

distractor_rationales.choice: The jacket soaks up warmth from the cold outside air and then passes that warmth on to her.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a jacket gathers warmth from its surroundings. The outside air is colder than she is, so energy flows from her to the air, not the reverse.
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a jacket collects heat from around it and gives it to the wearer

real_world_check: Insulating materials that trap still air reduce the rate of thermal energy transfer from warmer to cooler objects (MS-PS3-3).
key_category: an explanation of how clothing keeps a body warm
